abstract: Quantifying morphology from 3D scans is increasingly central to comparative biology, yet many existing pipelines require labor-intensive manual landmarking and impose strict assumptions on the data quality, hindering the high-throughput analysis of large and often imperfect digitized collections. In this work, we develop a fully unsupervised geometric framework that extracts robust parametric descriptors of cranial morphology directly from imperfect 3D skull meshes. Specifically, utilizing tools in computational geometry, differential geometry, and numerical optimization, the framework automatically aligns each specimen, measures the primary skull dimensions, and fits geometric primitives to the orbit and the neurocranium via robust iterative schemes, yielding stable estimates even for topologically noisy or damaged meshes. We demonstrate the framework on 100 skull specimens of Darwin's finches and their relatives. The extracted measurements recover the well-established scaling relationship between skull size and orbit curvature, providing a biological validation of the automated pipeline. Building on this, we establish a predictive model that estimates the orbit curvature from three easily obtainable linear skull measurements, explaining 86.36% of the variance in curvature with an average prediction error of only 6.14%, and further derive dimensionless relative-geometry descriptors that are invariant to uniform scaling and retain variation among the sampled genera. We also demonstrate the generalizability of our method by applying it to other avian and mammalian skulls. Altogether, our work establishes a rigorous foundation for the digital estimation and high-throughput phenotyping of large-scale museum collections without the need for manual landmarking.
